prayer.text: Saint Thomas Aquinas, pray for us.

cues.text: The Dumb Ox
Born around 1225 at the family castle of Roccasecca, near Aquino in the Kingdom of Sicily, Thomas came from a noble family connected to the imperial house of Hohenstaufen.

His family sent him as a child oblate to the great abbey of Monte Cassino, expecting he would eventually become its abbot—a comfortable, prestigious ecclesiastical career entirely in keeping with his aristocratic birth.
Thomas's own plans diverged sharply from his family's expectations.
While studying at the University of Naples, he encountered the new Dominican order.

Against every family interest, he resolved to join this recently founded order of mendicant preachers, whose radical poverty and academic rigor appealed far more than the comfortable monastic future his relatives had assumed.
A large, quiet, unusually reserved young man, Thomas was nicknamed "the Dumb Ox" by fellow students who mistook his silence for slowness.
A later tradition attributes to his teacher, Albert the Great , the prediction that this apparently slow ox's bellowing would one day be heard throughout the whole world.
A Family's Desperate Resistance
Thomas's family was scandalized that a son of their rank would join a mendicant order of preaching friars rather than a respectable and prestigious monastery.
They physically intercepted him as he traveled toward Paris and held him captive in the family castle for over a year, hoping to break his resolve.
When persuasion and confinement alike failed, his brothers reportedly sent a woman into his chamber to seduce him from his vocation.
Tradition holds that Thomas drove her from the room with a burning brand seized from the fireplace.
His family's resistance eventually collapsed before his sheer determination, and he was permitted to resume his Dominican formation.
A Vast Theological Synthesis
Thomas's mature career was spent teaching and writing at Paris, Rome, and Naples.
It produced one of the most ambitious and enduring theological achievements in the whole history of Christian thought: the Summa Theologiae .
This comprehensive, systematically organized treatment of the entire Christian faith stood alongside the earlier Summa Contra Gentiles and extensive biblical commentary and philosophical writing.
Thomas's genius lay above all in his careful integration of the newly rediscovered philosophy of Aristotle with the full inheritance of Christian revelation.
Recently reintroduced to Western Europe through Arabic and Byzantine scholarship, this philosophy became part of that integration.

Thomas demonstrated with painstaking rigor that reason and faith, rightly understood, could never genuinely contradict one another, since both flowed ultimately from the same single source of all truth.
A Method of Patient, Rigorous Argument
The distinctive method of the Summa — posing a question and presenting the strongest possible objections — reflects Thomas's deep intellectual integrity.

Only then does it offer a carefully reasoned resolution that took those objections seriously rather than dismissing them, expressing his conviction that truth need never fear a fair hearing of its strongest opposing arguments.

This method, and the vast systematic clarity it produced, would shape Catholic theological and philosophical education for the next seven centuries, and remains, to this day, a living and actively studied tradition within the Church.
"It Seems Like Straw to Me"
On December 6, 1273, while celebrating Mass, Thomas experienced a profound mystical encounter that left him permanently altered.
When his companion and secretary, Reginald of Piperno, urged him to continue his unfinished writing, Thomas replied that he could write no more.
Everything he had produced now seemed to him like straw compared to what had been revealed to him.
He never resumed significant writing, leaving his great Summa unfinished.
Legacy
Thomas died at the Cistercian abbey of Fossanova on March 7, 1274, while traveling to the Council of Lyon , only about forty-eight years old.
Canonized in 1323 and declared a Doctor of the Church, Thomas Aquinas was honored with the title Doctor Angelicus , the "Angelic Doctor."

He remains one of the most influential theologians in the history of Western Catholicism, his patient reconciliation of faith and reason still forming Catholic philosophy and theology's intellectual backbone.
His legacy rests not on the great final vision that silenced him, but on decades of quiet, disciplined labor that wrongly earned him the name of an ox too dull to speak.
